asDecan.p: Every sign gets split into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice has a ruling planet and a small card of its own. Your Sun is somewhere in the first ten degrees of Sagittarius, and in the Golden Dawn order that slice belongs to Mercury. Sagittarius is mutable fire ruled by Jupiter, the sign of the long view and the big question. Mercury's home is Gemini, the sign straight across the zodiac, so in Sagittarius it's in detriment. That just means it's working against the grain of the place, and you can see the effort. Gemini wants every detail and Sagittarius wants the headline, and you've got both of them in there having it out. The Nine of Wands comes next, the Moon's slice, someone bandaged and wary at the gate. Then Saturn and the Ten, a man bent under a bundle of sticks. Yours comes first, before anyone's tired. Temperance is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You talk fast, and you've probably been told so more than once. In a meeting you're three steps ahead of whoever's presenting and already asking about the thing on slide nine. At a family dinner you'll start a story about a trip to Lisbon, wander off into the history of the trams, and come back twenty minutes later to find everyone's moved on to dessert. You read the first chapter of four books in the same week. A friend texts you a simple question and gets a voice note that runs to six minutes. Mercury in Sagittarius is quick and sure of itself, and it tends to jump to the conclusion before the evidence has quite caught up. Most of the time you land on your feet, to be honest. You'd rather book the flight and work it out when you get there.

The thing people don't always credit you for is that you can explain things. Sit a nervous friend in front of a tax form, or give you a new colleague who can't see why the project matters, and you'll find the one sentence that makes it click. Teachers, tour guides, the uncle at the barbecue who explains the offside rule so a nine-year-old gets it first go, that's this decan working well. You also get bored of bad news quickly, which sounds like a flaw and often isn't. After a rough week you're usually the one in the group chat who's already found something funny about it, and your friends lean on that more than they'd say. When a plan falls through at the last minute, you've usually got a second one before anyone else has finished complaining.

The quieter problem is that you say things before you've checked them. Mercury in detriment gets the gist right and the specifics wrong, and you'll pass on a fact at a dinner party with total confidence and find out on the drive home it was a different country, or a different decade. Mostly that's harmless. It stops being harmless when it's about a person. You'll tell a friend what you reckon their partner meant, or sum up a colleague's situation to your boss in one breezy line, and that summary sticks to them for months. You can be tactless in a way you honestly don't notice, too. Someone shows you their new haircut and you say what you think, fast and cheerful, and then you're puzzled when they go quiet for the rest of the evening.

When something goes wrong your first move is to talk. You ring three people in an hour and tell the story a slightly different way each time, trying to find the version that makes sense of it. Then you start planning, usually something big, a new job, a move interstate, a course in something you've never mentioned before. A week later the plans have multiplied, none of them has started, and you're sleeping badly because your head won't stop running through them at two in the morning. The people close to you hear the same story over and over, which wears them out, and they can tell you're somewhere else. What helps is getting your body moving and your mouth quiet for a while. A long walk with no podcast. After that, pick one of the plans and do the first boring step of it.

You fall for people who can keep up in conversation, and a first date with you can easily run to four hours and three venues. What's less obvious is how badly you need things said straight. Hints go right past you. A partner who sighs and says it's fine will be believed, cheerfully, for weeks, and then you're properly hurt to find out it was never fine at all. You also need room to go off on your own, a weekend away with a mate, an evening at a talk about Roman roads, and you come back warmer for it. The trouble starts when you forget to tell anyone where you've gone. Send the message from the airport. It saves a lot of explaining on the way home.

You do best where you're allowed to move around and talk to people. Publishing, teaching, tourism, sales across time zones, anything with an international desk or a conference circuit. A job that keeps you at the same screen doing the same checks every day will wear you down within a year, and you'll be drafting your resignation in your head during the Monday stand-up. You're very good in the first week of a project, when nobody knows what it is yet and someone needs to write the pitch. You're weaker in the ninth month, when the contract has to be read line by line. That's the detriment showing, and it's fine as long as you know it. Find the colleague who loves the fine print and make a friend of them. Let them check your numbers before anything goes to the client.

At twenty this slice of Sagittarius is usually all motion. Backpacking, two degrees started and one finished, strong opinions about countries you've spent four days in. You're funny and good company and hard to pin down, and what you want to do with your life changes every six months or so. By the mid-thirties most people with this decan have learnt, often the embarrassing way, that being quick and being right are two separate things, and they start checking. The speed stays. What changes is that you let an email sit overnight before you send it. The fifties often bring a kind of authority, the person whose explanations get trusted because they've clearly been around. A lot of early Sagittarians I've seen end up teaching or writing, or leading the tour they used to tag along on.

Before you send any message that says something about another person, an email to your manager, a text in the family chat, a voice note about a friend's break-up, wait for as long as it takes to boil the kettle. Then read it through once and check one fact in it. Just one, the name, the date, what they actually said. If it holds up, send it. If it doesn't, fix that line and leave the rest alone.
